title: Sharp Transition-Contrast Bounds for Binary Panels with Attrition, Refreshment Samples, and Unknown Links
banked_reason: D0.5 assessed subfield below the field floor with no in-scope field repair, and the validity gate found unrepaired counterexamples making the current artifact not sound.
gap_reasons: Exact population decision procedures lack implementation/runtime evidence; broader calibration, numerical behavior, and sampling uncertainty would require material scope expansion.
All five findings remain unrepaired, so the note is not presently established as sound and must not be treated as an accepted result.
proof_attempt_summary: The run derived a binary reduction, finite endpoint decision procedure, local-width law, curvature breakdown, and a full varying-link comparator envelope, and it repaired an early empty-model defect. D0.5 then found two counterexample-bearing declarations plus three further dependency, tail, and comparator defects; repairing them could yield a sound subfield artifact but cannot meet the field floor without materially expanding the research program.
tldr: For binary panels with attrition and a representative refreshment sample, the normalized bounded-slope, bounded-curvature inverse-link class has a sharp transition-contrast interval with exact compatibility, endpoint, and tail certificates. Allowing the known link in Franguridi and Kosenkova (2026) to vary over its entire published family gives an exact binary order envelope, attained by smooth regular links. A same-observed-law example shows that two named links give positive contrasts while other published-admissible links give zero and negative contrasts. The bounded-class curvature frontier reaches zero at \(K=10/3\) in the critical rational law.
gap: The known-link event-threshold formula gives one completion, while unrestricted attriter coupling gives a broad benchmark. Neither supplies the sharp set over a shared, normalized inverse-link class with free tails and legal full-data and attriter cells.
fill: Establish exact feasibility and sharp endpoint certification, a usable active-regime solver, invariance conditions, and an interpretable curvature breakdown frontier.
